claims.text: Selective chemical dealloying of a multimetal precursor containing noble and less-noble elements can produce HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
The initial precursor is a homogeneous alloy of noble and less-noble metals.
Chemical dealloying is performed in an electrolytic solution under controlled pH and temperature.
Adjusting electrolyte composition, temperature, and pH can preferentially leach the less-noble elements.
Controlled dealloying preserves a connected noble-metal scaffold.
The surviving noble-metal network acts as a scaffold that directs formation of a three-dimensional porous framework.
Selective extraction of less-stable elements creates vacancies.
Selective extraction of less-stable elements creates channels.
Vacancy and channel formation allows the remaining noble metals to reorganize into an interconnected three-dimensional structure.
The resulting three-dimensional structure has high surface area.
Dealloying will form complex, porous HEA nanoframeworks.
The HEA nanoframeworks may have enhanced catalytic properties relative to the non-dealloyed precursor.
The untreated precursor lacks the high surface area of the proposed nanoframework.
The untreated precursor lacks a structurally organized nanoframework.
Framework-formation efficiency depends strongly on alloy composition and dealloying conditions.
Overly aggressive dealloying conditions may collapse the framework.
Conditions that are too mild may fail to create the desired porosity.

contradictions.description: The core hypothesis concerns formation of a 3D nanoframework, and catalytic enhancement is described only as potential; however, the falsification rule treats a lack of significantly improved catalytic performance as sufficient to refute the hypothesis even if a nanoframework forms.
